content: Biotin is a vitamin that has received FDA approval for its role in strengthening hair follicles and preventing hair loss. It serves as a nutrient for the hair root, aiding in oxygenation, which slows hair loss and enhances hair resilience and resistance. Common side effects include gastrointestinal upset, and the use of anticonvulsant medications may interfere with biotin absorption. For adults, biotin is applied directly to the hair follicle and massaged until absorbed. This application is recommended every 12 hours for rapid and sustained effects. Biotin is suitable for use across all age groups, including children, adolescents, adults, and seniors. Off-label uses of biotin in adults include: For biotinidase deficiency: 10 to 40 milligrams daily, taken orally. For brittle nails: 2.5 milligrams daily, taken orally in tablet form. For carboxylase deficiency: 18.4 micromoles daily, administered intravenously. For holocarboxylase deficiency during pregnancy: 10 milligrams daily, taken orally. For parenteral alimentation-induced deficiency: 0.1 to 1 milligram daily, taken orally as a solution or tablet. For general dietary supplementation: 30 to 100 micrograms daily, taken orally. For vaginal candidiasis: 20 milligrams daily, taken orally. In pediatric patients, there is limited FDA-labeled information regarding biotin use. However, off-label uses include: For alopecia areata: 20 milligrams daily, taken orally, combined with oral zinc aspartate (100 milligrams) and topical clobetasol propionate (0.025%). For biotin-responsive basal ganglia disease: 5 to 10 milligrams per kilogram daily, taken orally or as a solution. For beta-methylcrotonyl-glycinuria: 10 milligrams daily, taken orally as a solution. For biotinidase deficiency: 6 to 40 milligrams daily, taken orally as a solution or tablet. For parenteral alimentation-induced deficiency: 0.1 to 1 milligram daily, taken orally as a solution or tablet. For partial biotinidase deficiency: 5 to 10 milligrams daily or less, taken orally as a solution or tablet. For protein-energy malnutrition: 10 milligrams daily, taken orally as a solution or tablet, alongside standard malnutrition treatment. For pyruvate-carboxylase deficiency: 10 milligrams daily, taken orally as a solution or tablet, along with thiamine (80 milligrams daily) and pyridoxine (300 milligrams daily). For uncombable hair syndrome: 0.9 milligrams daily, taken orally in three divided doses. Biotin is contraindicated in individuals with hypersensitivity to the substance. If the product comes into contact with the eyes, it should be rinsed immediately with water, and medical advice should be sought. Adverse reactions reported include gastrointestinal upset. Additionally, anticonvulsant medications may impair the absorption of biotin. There is no specific FDA guidance on the use of biotin during pregnancy, labor and delivery, nursing, or in pediatric, geriatric, gender-specific, racial, renal-impaired, hepatic-impaired, or immunocompromised populations. Biotin is administered orally, and there is limited information available regarding its monitoring, IV compatibility, chronic overdose, mechanism of action, structure, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, nonclinical toxicology, and clinical studies. The interaction between alcohol and biotin has not been established. Patients are advised to consult their healthcare provider regarding the effects of alcohol consumption while taking biotin. Biotin is marketed under the brand name BIONA-VIT®.
